circularConcentration.basis: Task 'periodic-measurement' (2026-08-18), REVISED after the first calibration attempt (a fixed R cutoff, minR=exp(-0.5)=0.6065) failed on this project's own real data -- see below. R is the mean resultant length of unit vectors formed by mapping one axis' own coordinates to angles theta=2*pi*x/box (Mardia & Jupp, 'Directional Statistics', Wiley 1999, ch.2): R=1 for every coordinate at the same angle, R=0 for angles uniformly spread around the full circle, i.e. the coordinate uniformly spread across the whole periodic box on that axis -- the exact failure mode this task's brief names ('a circular mean is meaningless if the object is uniformly spread along an axis'). A FIXED high-R cutoff, though a standard textbook notion (circular standard deviation sigma_circ=sqrt(-2*ln(R)), same reference ch.2.3), turned out to conflate two different claims: 'this axis carries no positional information at all' (the real failure mode) versus 'this object is large relative to the box' (not a failure at all). By Archimedes' 'hat-box' theorem, the projection of a uniformly-sampled SPHERE surface onto any one axis is itself exactly uniform on [-r,r] -- so a real, well-defined, non-degenerate hollow spherical shell whose OWN diameter is already a large-but-sub-box fraction (measured on this task's own synthetic validation shell, diameter/box=0.688: R~=0.38) sits far below a fixed R=0.6065 bar despite being a perfectly good, non-wraparound object with a well-defined location -- and this project's own real dense-campaign checkpoints (measured, tests/periodic-measurement.test.ts's own calibration pass: R in [0.17, 0.37] across all three axes and all ten checkpoints) sit in the exact same regime. A fixed-R bar would therefore refuse a centre for every real checkpoint this task exists to measure, which is not the brief's intent (its own hole/profile/cavity measurements all presume a centre WAS obtained). Replaced with the textbook-correct tool for the actual null hypothesis ('this axis is statistically indistinguishable from uniform'): Rayleigh's test for circular uniformity (same reference, sec 6.3.1; Fisher, 'Statistical Analysis of Circular Data', 1993, sec 5.3.1) -- under H0 (n unit vectors uniformly distributed on the circle), 2*n*R^2 is approximately chi-square-distributed with 2 degrees of freedom, giving the large-sample approximation p ~= exp(-n*R^2). Solving for R at significance level alpha gives R_min(n) = sqrt(-ln(alpha)/n): SMALLER for MORE points (more samples make a smaller true concentration statistically detectable), the opposite of a fixed bar, and the property that correctly separates the two claims above -- a huge, genuinely non-uniform object with many members (R modest, n large) still clears it, while a genuinely uniform axis with few or many points does not (this task's own synthetic validation: n=4000 deliberately uniform points measured R=0.0085; R_min(4000, 1e-6)=0.0588, so it is correctly refused). alpha=1e-6 is set well beyond even a conservative Bonferroni correction for this task's own repeated real-data testing (3 axes x 10 checkpoints = 30 tests; the naive corrected bar would be 0.05/30~=0.0017, several orders above 1e-6) -- a false 'trusted' verdict from sampling noise alone is essentially ruled out.
